beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The generator sharpens against that feedback while you walk away.
beats.got: Something checks the output and something else improves it, without me. No cost, no risk, no payback.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: There is reading, and I am supposed to have a judge from last time. I did not do the reading.

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** the one-off Module 5 judge from one that runs on every output
beats.got: One judge used by hand, one judge used automatically. That much is clear.

beats.trigger: can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: An academic question I have not been asked by anyone with a budget.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: The system fixes itself while I am not there. That is either a saving or a control problem, and no figure says which.

beats.trigger: Humans will not cope with all the detail for long.
beats.got: People can't check everything, so the checking gets written down. I can accept that.

beats.trigger: The same claim pool went through the same evidence, and the scoreboard named which method caught the misses.
beats.got: A benchmark compares methods on identical input and a scoreboard shows the winner. That is how I test things.

beats.trigger: every number traces to a file
beats.got: The first check is that every figure ties back to a source. That is just audit trail logic.

beats.trigger: Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.
beats.got: Correct is not the same as useful. But 'overperform' is a soft target, and I would ask who defines it.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: Rule changes and the measure changes together, so the trend is worthless. This is why we freeze the budget method before comparing periods. The byte-identical check is a control I can verify.

beats.trigger: The eval checks the thing that matters, at the moment where the mistake would hurt, against a standard you would defend.
beats.got: Pick the check carefully and be able to defend it. Fair, but it comes with no example.

beats.trigger: **Time:** 45 min: manual run ~5, walk-away ~30, return and read notes ~10.
beats.got: Forty-five minutes is a real cost, and it is spent on a generic briefing, not on my material.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: I ran it once by hand and saw what it flags. It is a checklist with a pass or fail per claim.

beats.trigger: Now step away. Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: Thirty minutes of waiting. I answered email. The parallel search and model-training questions felt like a detour.

beats.trigger: the SHA in `module-6/eval-notes.md` must match.
beats.got: There is a fingerprint on the judge file. If it matches, nobody moved the yardstick. That is a control I can check myself.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Each round it learned from the last one's flagged claims. The trend is visible.

beats.trigger: You do not inspect every output; you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: My job moves from checking each output to owning the standard. That is how internal control works too.

beats.trigger: Convergence was the floor in Module 5. Eval-as-yardstick is the ceiling here.
beats.got: Any judge can go into the loop. I have no idea which of my processes that would be.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: A zero count on the flags does not mean the work is good.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: If the KPI stops moving, the KPI may be too narrow. Every board pack has green metrics that miss the point.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Nothing audits the auditor yet. Hand-score a sample against the judge once, and don't let the generator mark its own work. That is segregation of duties.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: The judge may become redundant when models improve. 'What good means' stays my job.

beats.trigger: The agent wrote a snake game.
beats.got: A recap of earlier modules. A snake game does not help me with a variance report.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A list of conditions before an agent may send anything. It reads like approval criteria.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem.
beats.got: Same floor and ceiling point again. I got it on the first pass.

beats.trigger: the generator makes more than you need, the judge discards most of it, and the tactic file keeps what survived.
beats.got: Make many, throw most away, keep the rule that worked. It is abstract, and I would want to know the cost of all that discarded output.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: Draft only, review first, or automatic once checks pass. It is a delegation-of-authority ladder, and some items always need sign-off. I can work with that.

beats.trigger: Create one steering eval for internal mail an agent could help with.
beats.got: Build a second judge for internal mail. I can't see why I would start with mail.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: A long run of clean reports makes you stop looking, and that is exactly how fraud and drift go unnoticed. This is the first risk named before I raised it.

beats.trigger: This check has no instrument, only a date
beats.got: Put a date in the calendar and read one output end to end yourself. That is a cheap, concrete control.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: Summary diagram and a nice line about autonomy. Nothing I can put in a deck.

beats.trigger: The judge file stays untouched: that's the integrity of the loop.
beats.got: Tell the agent to sharpen the tactic and keep the judge untouched.

beats.trigger: Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines.
beats.got: Challenge the agent's summary and make it show the evidence. That is a normal question for a CFO.

beats.trigger: You design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: Four points I could repeat. None of them has a number.

beats.trigger: **Monday's first five agent calls, written down**
beats.got: Homework: five calls written down. I will ask my controller for them.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: Trust what you can inspect. I agree with that.

take_homes: If the yardstick changes, the score is worthless. Freeze the judge, change only the work, and check the file fingerprint.
Nobody has checked the judge. Hand-score a sample against it once, and never let the generator grade itself.
The more it runs clean, the less you look. Put a date in the calendar and read one output myself.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run the month-end variance commentary through a generate-and-judge loop once. A second person hand-scores ten of the outputs against the judge.
monday.who: Controller, plus one analyst for the hand-scoring
monday.when: Month-end close, if IT allows it. Not before.
monday.stop_condition: The judge and the analyst disagree on more than a couple of the ten, or the monthly licence and time cost for 40 people is not stated and defensible.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and nobody has told me what this costs.

misconception.why: The module talks about capability, loops and who owns the yardstick, but it never gives a cost or payback. I still read AI as a licence plus a risk to control. The judge-checking and 'read one yourself' beats shook it slightly, because they show this needs people with standards, not only a purchase.

one_line: Good on controls: freeze the yardstick, check the checker, keep reading the output. But 45 minutes on a generic briefing and not one figure on cost or payback.
